reproductions.title: ERASOR: Egocentric Ratio of Pseudo Occupancy-Based Dynamic Object Removal for Static 3D Point Cloud Map Building
reproductions.heading: 01-03 · ERASOR

checks.name: reproduces_benchmark_row
checks.detail: SA/DA/AA = 66.71/98.54/81.07 vs DynamicMap_Benchmark Table I 66.7/98.54/81.07, within 0.5 pp

checks.name: output_is_voxel_downsampled
checks.detail: the cleaned map holds 1417955 points against 17362230 GT points - ERASOR's MapUpdater voxelises at 0.1 m, so most 'false removals' are downsampling, not deletion

findings.name: low_SA_is_downsampling_not_deletion
findings.detail: SA 66.71% with 5748315 GT points marked removed, yet DA is 98.54%. The map has 12.2x fewer points than the GT cloud, so the 0.05 m nearest-neighbour rule reads downsampling as removal. The benchmark's metric therefore penalises resolution, not correctness - worth remembering before calling any method 'worse'.

findings.name: same_method_27_points_apart_across_metrics
findings.detail: ERASOR scores PR 93.980 on its own voxel-wise metric (SemanticKITTI 00, Table II p.8) and SA 66.71 on the benchmark's point-wise metric (KITTI 00). Removert goes the other way: 85.502 -> 99.44. The ranking between the two methods inverts with the metric.

reproductions.title: Removert: Remove then Revert — Static Map Building in Challenging Environment
reproductions.heading: 01-04 · Removert

checks.name: reproduces_benchmark_row
checks.detail: SA/DA/AA = 99.44/41.53/64.26 vs DynamicMap_Benchmark Table I 99.44/41.53/64.26, within 0.5 pp

checks.name: removert_is_the_conservative_extreme
checks.detail: SA 99.44% with only DA 41.53% - it keeps essentially the whole map (56120 dynamic GT points left in) rather than risk deleting static structure

findings.name: original_paper_is_unobtainable
findings.detail: Removert's IROS 2020 paper is closed access: OpenAlex returns is_oa=false, oa_status=closed, any_repository_has_fulltext=false, and the authors' own link (irap.kaist.ac.kr) fails DNS. So the target here is the benchmark's reimplementation, not Removert's self-reported numbers - the only folder in this repo where that is true.

findings.name: the_two_extremes_disagree_about_what_good_means
findings.detail: Removert SA 99.44 / DA 41.53 against ERASOR's 66.71 / 98.54 on the same data and the same metric. They are opposite corners: one refuses to delete, the other deletes too much. AA ranks them DUFOMap > ERASOR > Removert, SA ranks them Removert > DUFOMap > ERASOR - the task book's ranking-stability question, answered on real numbers.

reproductions.title: DUFOMap: Efficient Dynamic Awareness Mapping
reproductions.static_status: 🟢 **已复现：与论文 2 位小数完全一致**
reproductions.heading: 01-05 · DUFOMap

checks.name: reproduces_paper_headline
checks.detail: d_p=1 gives SA/DA/AA = 97.96/98.72/98.34 vs paper 97.96/98.72/98.34 (Table I p.5), within 0.5 pp

checks.name: gt_is_binary_and_rare_dynamic
checks.detail: GT = 17266247 static + 95983 dynamic points (0.55% dynamic) - a rare-positive problem, so AA is dominated by SA

checks.name: dp_is_load_bearing
checks.detail: d_p=2 keeps +1.92 pp more static and removes -2.09 pp fewer dynamic points than the paper's d_p=1

findings.name: upstream_example_contradicts_the_paper
findings.detail: DynamicMap_Benchmark's methods/dufomap/main.py passes d_p=2 with the comment 'same with paper', but the DUFOMap paper's default - the one whose Table I row we reproduce - is d_p=1 (Table IV, p.7). Using the example's value reproduces AA only by coincidence; SA and DA are each off by about 2 pp.

findings.name: geometric_mean_hides_the_sa_da_tradeoff
findings.detail: d_p=1 -> SA 97.96 / DA 98.72 / AA 98.34; d_p=2 -> SA 99.89 / DA 96.63 / AA 98.25. The two AA values are 0.09 pp apart while SA and DA each move ~2 pp in opposite directions - the geometric mean of a rare-positive problem is almost entirely SA, so it cannot tell a conservative cleaner from an aggressive one.

findings.name: dynamic_points_are_0_55_percent_of_the_map
findings.detail: 95983 of 17362230 GT points are dynamic; any metric averaged over points is therefore a static-preservation metric in disguise.

reproductions.note: DUFOMap on KITTI 00: SA/DA/AA = 97.96/98.72/98.34 vs paper 97.96/98.72/98.34

reproductions.title: BeautyMap: Binary-Encoded Adaptable Ground Matrix for Dynamic Points Removal in Global Maps
reproductions.heading: 01-06 · BeautyMap

checks.name: reproduces_paper_row
checks.detail: SA/DA/HA = 96.95/98.34/97.64 vs BeautyMap Table I p.6 96.76/98.38/97.56, within 0.5 pp

checks.name: aa_and_ha_agree_only_because_sa_da_are_close
checks.detail: AA 97.6431 vs HA 97.6407 - the two means differ by 0.0024 pp here because SA and DA are within 1.4 pp of each other. That is a property of this method on this sequence, not of the metrics.

findings.name: upstream_does_not_run_on_numpy_2
findings.detail: BeautyMap's vendored utils/pcdpy3.py calls np.fromstring (line 150) and ndarray.tostring (line 265), both removed in NumPy 2. Two LOCAL PATCHed lines (frombuffer(...).copy() and tobytes(order='C')) are required. The first failure is at read time; the second only after ~50 s of processing, at write time - a fresh clone that patches only the first looks fine until it has done all the work.

findings.name: matches_the_benchmark_papers_HA_column_too
findings.detail: This run also reproduces the HA column that the BeautyMap paper prints for the other methods: Removert 41.53/58.59 and ERASOR 98.54/79.55 predicted from this paper's Table I, and measured here as 41.5313/58.591 and 98.5352/79.5563. Two papers and four methods now agree on the same numbers, which is the strongest evidence we have that the whole data-and-evaluation chain is right.

findings.name: beautymap_is_the_balanced_one
findings.detail: BeautyMap SA 96.95 / DA 98.34 sits between Removert's refuse-to-delete (99.44/41.53) and ERASOR's delete-too-much (66.71/98.54), and is the only one of the four with both above 96.

reproductions.note: BeautyMap on KITTI 00: SA/DA/HA = 96.95/98.34/97.64 vs paper 96.76/98.38/97.56

reproductions.title: NGD-SLAM: Towards Real-Time Dynamic SLAM without GPU
reproductions.static_status: 🟢 **已复现：ATE 与 RPE-平移命中论文**；RPE-旋转有一处未解差异
reproductions.heading: 01-08 · NGD-SLAM

checks.name: reproduces_paper_ate
checks.detail: ATE (rigid, no scale) = 0.0157 m vs paper 0.015 m (Table I p.5, f3/walking_xyz), within 0.003

checks.name: reproduces_paper_rpe_translation
checks.detail: RPE translation = 0.0201 m/s vs paper 0.02 m/s, within 0.003

checks.name: every_frame_was_processed
checks.detail: 827 poses written; the paper requires processing all 827 frames, and both mechanisms (mask propagation and optical flow) depend on frame-to-frame continuity

findings.name: rotational_rpe_depends_on_an_unspecified_convention
findings.detail: our rotational RPE is 0.604 °/s by RMSE but 0.475 °/s by mean, against the paper's 0.47 °/s. The column is headed only 'RPE rotation (°/s)'. The distribution is skewed (median far below the max), which is exactly when the choice matters. Translation shows the same asymmetry but much smaller, so it happens to agree either way.

findings.name: cheap_semantics_is_the_actual_contribution
findings.detail: reading the official source, the system DOES use a neural network (YOLO-fastest-xl at 320x320, System.cc:217) - what it removes is the tracker's dependency on waiting for it (Tracking.cc:1592 never blocks, Tracking.cc:4286 propagates the old mask with LK optical flow). So it is a scheduling result, not a geometry-only result, and it inherits COCO's blind spot for unknown dynamic objects.

findings.name: wall_clock_is_the_same_order_as_the_paper
findings.detail: mean tracking 20.76 ms/frame vs the paper's 16.72 ms (~60 FPS). Measured headless on different hardware, so this supports 'same order of magnitude on CPU', not an exact match.

reproductions.note: NGD-SLAM on TUM fr3/walking_xyz: ATE 0.0157 m vs paper 0.015 m; RPE trans 0.0201 m/s vs 0.02
